create.name: Three Kingdoms Banqi: Level 7 versus Level 8, annotated
create.description: A recorded engine game, analyzed with the served Level 8 engine and pinned net. Flip choices use public pool means; reveal luck is separate. From mistboard.com/rules/three-kingdoms-banqi.

comments.text: The black chariot on h2 takes the red elephant on h1. Its 5 points bring Level 7 from 95 to 100, which wins the game, 100 to 45. Seven pieces are still face down, and the study never shows what they are.
The black horse on g5 takes the red chariot on f3, right after that chariot took another black horse. The chariot is worth 15 and the lost horse 10, so Level 7 comes out ahead, 90 to 45.

The flip on i1 turns up the second red chariot. It is a strong piece but scores nothing by itself: Level 8 still trails 20 to 55. Averaged over the pieces still face down, the flip was worth 3.7% for Level 8; this chariot gives 3.6%, so the draw changes little.

The red soldier on e2 takes the black chariot on e3. In Three Kingdoms any piece may take any piece it reaches, so a soldier can take a chariot. Level 8 scores its first 15 points; the score is 15 to 45.

The black cannon on h2 jumps the face-down piece on g2 to take the red horse on e2. The red chariot has left f2, so g2 is the only piece in between. The capture adds 10 points for Level 7, and the jumped piece stays unknown.

The flip on f2 turns up a red chariot. Before the flip, the analysis preferred moving the red horse from e2 to f4, by 4.0 percentage points. The side line shows that move, chosen without knowing what f2 held.

The black chariot takes the red cannon on g4. Level 7 already has 5 points for the red advisor; the cannon adds 10, for 15. Captures score the points, and the first to 100 wins, so rank alone does not decide this game.

The opening flip turns up a red advisor on f4, so Level 8 plays red and Level 7 plays black. Averaged over every piece still face down, this flip was worth 54.8% for Level 8; the advisor gives 53.7%. The grade judges the choice of point, and the die judges the draw.

Level 8 moves first and plays red; Level 7 plays black and wins on points. The graph shows Level 8’s winning chances. A flip’s grade compares it with the average over every piece still face down; the die shows whether the piece that turned up was a lucky draw. Pieces still face down stay unknown throughout.
